opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I find genuinely fascinating, partly because of my background in physical simulation. When you build a simulator, say for fluids or elastic materials, you make a lot of choices: how you discretize space, what time step you use, whether you use a grid or particles, how you handle numerical precision. Every one of those choices leaves fingerprints in the simulated world.

So if you're a creature living inside, for example, a grid-based fluid simulation, in principle you might notice some strange things. Maybe the physics isn't perfectly rotationally invariant, because the grid has preferred directions. Maybe there's some numerical dissipation, so energy slowly disappears in ways that don't match any clean conservation law. Maybe at very small scales, things get blocky or behave weirdly near the resolution limit. These are artifacts we, as simulation engineers, spend a lot of effort trying to hide, but they're very hard to eliminate completely.

The interesting part is that from the inside, you'd have no "ground truth" to compare against. You'd just think, "Well, this is how physics works." The artifacts would just become your laws of nature. So the real question is whether you can find something that looks *unnatural*, something that seems too arbitrary or too much like an engineering compromise, like a hard cutoff, a maximum speed of information propagation, or quantization at some fundamental scale.

And it's funny, because when you look at our own universe, some features do have that flavor. There's a speed limit, the speed of light, which is a bit like a CFL condition in a numerical solver: information can't travel more than some number of cells per time step. There's quantization. There's the Planck scale. I'm not saying that's evidence we're in a simulation. Those features have very elegant physical explanations. But as someone who writes simulators, I can't help noticing the resemblance.

I think the honest answer is that a well-designed simulation, or one computed at a much higher level of fidelity than anything its inhabitants can probe, would be essentially undetectable. You can only detect the computation where the designer cut corners. So the inhabitants' best strategy would be to look for the corners: the edge cases, the extreme regimes, the places where conservation laws seem to bend slightly. That's basically what physicists already do, just with a different motivation.

And for me, there's a more practical takeaway: when I build simulation tools, I'm essentially building small worlds. Thinking about what an inhabitant would notice is a pretty good way to think about what makes a simulation good, meaning which artifacts matter and which ones nobody would ever see.

r001.rationale: The response discusses detectable simulation artifacts, but says nothing about unobserved objects or distinguishing continuous evolution from updates at observation.

r002.rationale: It does not propose that observing many objects could increase computational workload or slow the simulated world.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that an in-world observer could not detect a slowdown because the observer is simulated too.

r004.rationale: It says a well-designed or sufficiently high-fidelity simulation would be essentially undetectable to its inhabitants, clearly expressing that they could have no way to discover it.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, actually, because I spend my days building the other side of it. With Taichi, with Genesis, I'm writing the code that computes a world, and then I watch things happen inside it that I didn't explicitly put there. Fluids splash, sand piles up, cloth folds. So the honest first answer is: from inside, you mostly can't tell. A simulated world is designed to look like it isn't one. That's the whole job.

But I'd push on "mostly." If you lived inside one of my simulations and were clever enough, there are fingerprints. The first is discretization. Everything I build runs on a grid or a set of particles with some finite resolution and a finite time step. Nothing is truly continuous. So if you could probe your world at very small scales and very short times, you'd find a floor, a smallest meaningful length, a smallest tick. Interestingly, our universe seems to have something like that too, the Planck scale, and I try not to read too much into that, but it is a fun coincidence.

The second fingerprint is numerical error. Simulations don't conserve things perfectly. Energy drifts, momentum leaks, and the pattern of that leakage tells you which integrator was used. Explicit Euler drifts one way, symplectic schemes wobble but stay bounded. So a physicist inside my world who measured tiny violations of conservation laws, and noticed they had structure rather than being random, would learn something about my solver.

The third one is the one I find most interesting, which is what gets cheated. Anyone who has built a real-time engine knows you never simulate everything at full fidelity. You use level of detail. Far away things are coarse, things nobody is looking at get frozen or approximated. So the deep test from inside would be: does reality get sloppier where observation is weaker? Does the world render lazily? That would be the signature of an engineer with a budget rather than a universe with infinite compute.

And then there's the uncomfortable flip side. The stuff I just described, a smallest scale, weird behavior when you measure, finite information in a region, our physics has all of it. Which either means we're in a simulation, or it means that any computable world has to look like this, and so these features are evidence of nothing in particular. I lean toward the second reading. Computation and physics may just be the same thing described twice.

So my practical answer is this. I don't think you can prove you're simulated from inside, because any evidence you find could be a law of nature rather than an implementation detail. But you can learn the constraints the world runs under, and those constraints are the same whether there's a programmer or not. Honestly, as someone who writes simulators, that makes me less interested in whether we're in one and more interested in the fact that the design space is so narrow. If I were building a universe, I'd probably end up with something that looks a lot like this one.

r001.rationale: It mentions objects being frozen or approximated when nobody is looking, but does not say their evolution is indistinguishable from updates made only when observed.

r002.rationale: It does not propose that observing many objects could increase computational workload and slow the world.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that an observer would fail to detect slowdown because the observer is simulated too.

r004.rationale: It says an observer cannot prove from inside that the world is simulated, since any evidence could also be a law of nature.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting question is whether the implementation leaves any observable traces. If two different programs produce exactly the same observations for someone inside the world, then you cannot distinguish them from inside. You can discover the rules of that world, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how those rules are computed.

For example, you might simulate a world using a grid. If that grid introduces some directional bias, someone inside could potentially measure it. But even then, finding that bias wouldn’t uniquely identify the program running the simulation. It would just give you another property of the world to explain.

So I would separate discovering the laws of a world from discovering its implementation. The first is something you can do through experiments. The second may be possible only to the extent that the implementation leaks into what you can observe.

r004.rationale: The response says implementation may be discoverable if it leaves observable traces; it does not propose that inhabitants could have no way to discover the world is simulated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is what information is actually observable from inside. If two different ways of computing a world produce exactly the same observations, then you can’t distinguish them. You can discover the rules of that world, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you how those rules are implemented.

You could look for clues—some limit on resolution, for example, or an approximation that behaves strangely in a particular situation. As someone building simulations, I know we make those tradeoffs all the time. But even if you found something like that, it would be difficult to say whether it was an artifact of the simulation or simply a law of physics you hadn’t understood yet.

So I would separate understanding the world’s behavior from understanding the computer underneath it. The first seems possible through experiments. The second might be impossible if the implementation never exposes itself.
